newsitem.title: USA: Canada pipeline cut disrupts September strategies.
newsitem.headline: Canada pipeline cut disrupts September strategies.

text.p: A reduction of nearly 10 percent in September throughput on Canada's main crude oil artery into the U.S. Midwest market has helped to boost prices for domestic sour crude, traders said.
The disruption also has U.S. importers of Canadian crude reviewing their shipping strategies and assessing the likely impact, both in the Midwest and on the West Coast.

IPL Energy Inc said last Friday it was planning maintenance on the line that would cut September crude throughput by about 141,000 barrels per day (bpd) on its Interprovincial Pipe Line system from a usual rate of 1.5 million bpd.

The Interprovincial line (Lakehead on the U.S. side) runs from Edmonton, Alberta through Superior, Wis. and Chicago to various points in southern Ontario - the world's longest crude oil and liquids pipeline system.

Though the throughput reduction represents only between one and two percent of total U.S. imports, U.S. oil dealers said it could have a local market impact as the cut was larger than had been expected.
The discount for West Texas Sour/Midland, for example, had narrowed to around $1.20 under U.S. benchmark West Texas Intermediate/Cushing by Tuesday, compared to $1.30 to $1.40 under in recent weeks.
One crude trader said the IPL news also had dampened trading in Canadian grades as buyers try to work out their strategies.
"This has stifled a bunch of activity with people not knowing the impact," the trader said.

Shippers have until early Wednesday to tell IPL how much crude they want to move through the line in September and then the operator will apportion the space accordingly. They are likley to ask for more space than needed and then assess the level of apportionment, the trader said.
Canadian traders had been expecting virtually no space rationing on IPL before the maintenance news as the system has enjoyed zero apportionment for months.
For Midwest buyers, the impact likely will be softened as other pipelines take up some of the slack.

The Express pipeline, which runs crude to Casper, Wyoming from Hardisty, Alberta has a design capacity of 172,000 bpd. The line, owned by Alberta Energy Co Ltd and TransCanada PipeLines Ltd, is currently running at 140,000 bpd, according to an Express spokesman.
The Platte pipeline extension runs crude from the Express terminus to lower Midwest destinations.

Arco's Seaway pipeline, which runs from Freeport, Texas north to Cushing, Oklahoma, where a number of other lines move crude through the central U.S., also has extra space. An Arco spokesman said Seaway has room on the 250,000 bpd capacity line in September.

The IPL restrictions are likely to force western Canadian oil producers to search for alternative markets for their ever-increasing output, especially as they have already suffered weather-related delays this year in getting their crude to market.
Buyers on the U.S. West Coast may benefit if, for example, nominations on the 250,000 barrel a day Trans Mountain pipeline to the west coast from Alberta, see a big increase, traders said.
The pipeline, owned by BC Gas Inc, would provide some relief for light/sweet and sour producers, they said.
((--Patrick Connole, New York Energy Desk, +1 212 859 1828; Jeff Jones, Calgary Bureau, +1 403 531 1624))
